ready1_open_rewrite.raw_question_text:
Certain fish achieve buoyancy control by adjusting the volume of their swim bladder. The swim bladder structure can be simplified as two closed air chambers, A and B, connected by a valve. Chamber A has thick walls and can be considered to have a constant volume, while chamber B has thin walls and a variable volume. The gas within both chambers is treated as an ideal gas and can be exchanged through the valve. A fish with mass $M$ is stationary at a depth $H$ below the water surface. The gas volume in chamber B is $V$ and its mass is $m$. Assume that the gas pressure in chamber B is equal to the external pressure on the fish, the change in fish volume is equal to the change in gas volume of chamber B, the fish mass remains constant, and the gas temperature in the swim bladder remains constant. The density of water is $\rho$ and the acceleration due to gravity is $g$. The atmospheric pressure is $p_{0}$.

1. The fish obtains an acceleration of magnitude $a$ by increasing the volume of chamber B, and the mass of gas $\Delta m$ needs to be transferred from chamber A to chamber B.
2. When the fish is stationary at a depth $H_{1}$ below the water surface, the mass of gas in chamber B is $m_{1}$.
ready1_open_rewrite.raw_answer_text:
$\Delta m=\frac{M m a}{V\rho g}$
$m_{1}=\frac{\rho g H_{1}+p_{0}}{\rho g H+p_{0}}m$

The density of water is $\rho$ and the acceleration due to gravity is $g$. The atmospheric pressure is $p_{0}$. 1. The fish obtains an acceleration of magnitude $a$ by increasing the volume of chamber B, and the mass of gas $\Delta m$ needs to be transferred from chamber A to chamber B. 2. ready2_open_rewrite.resolved_answer: $\Delta m=\frac{M m a}{V\rho g}$ $m_{1}=\frac{\rho g H_{1}+p_{0}}{\rho g H+p_{0}}m$
ready2_open_rewrite.final_cot: Image description: In the attached figure, on the left is a thin-walled elliptical gas chamber labeled B; on the right is a thick-walled, approximately rounded-rectangle gas chamber labeled A; between the two there is a section of connecting tube, and at the connection it is labeled valve (valve). Therefore, when gas is transferred between A and B through the valve, the thick-walled A can be regarded as having unchanged volume, and the volume of the thin-walled B can change. Reasoning: The fish was originally at rest at a depth H below the water surface, and the gas pressure in chamber B is equal to the external water pressure, so p=p_0+\rho gH. The initial rest indicates that gravity and buoyancy are balanced. If the volume of chamber B increases by \Delta V, the volume of water displaced by the fish also increases by \Delta V, therefore the increase in buoyancy is \rho g\Delta V. The fish therefore obtains an acceleration of magnitude a, and the extra resultant force is Ma, hence \rho g\Delta V=Ma, giving \Delta V=Ma/(\rho g). At the same depth and with temperature unchanged, the pressure of chamber B is unchanged, and the ideal gas satisfies that mass is proportional to volume, namely \Delta m/m=\Delta V/V. Therefore \Delta m=m\Delta V/V=Mm a/(V\rho g). When the fish is again at rest at depth H_1, since the mass of the fish is unchanged, the volume of the non-gas part is unchanged, and the total displaced-water volume required when at rest is still determined by M/\rho, the volume of chamber B is still equal to the original V. At this time the external pressure is p_1=p_0+\rho gH_1. The temperature and the volume of chamber B are the same, and the ideal gas mass is proportional to pressure, so m_1/m=(p_0+\rho gH_1)/(p_0+\rho gH).
